title: Early Defense vs Late Defense
shortDefinition: Early defense addresses body signals before the position locks; late defense deals with force already applied.
whyItMatters: Modern no-gi is fast: early defense saves energy and is much safer.
deepExplanation: Early defense is chin tuck before chin strap, knee-line escape before heel exposure, elbow-knee before chest-to-chest. Late defense is not forbidden, but dangerous force requires early tap or reset.
beginnerView: Recognize early signals instead of waiting for pain or choke.
advancedView: Build cue systems for each danger line: neck, knee line, shoulder line, back exposure.

ifThenExamples.if: If you lose Early Defense vs Late Defense during the exchange.
ifThenExamples.then: Stop accelerating, recover the nearest body structure, then continue the technique.
ifThenExamples.why: Modern no-gi punishes forceful continuation after structure is lost.

ifThenExamples.if: If the opponent correctly answers your first line.
ifThenExamples.then: Use Early Defense vs Late Defense to switch to a safer branch instead of forcing the same line.
ifThenExamples.why: A good concept turns the opponent’s reaction into information for the next decision.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Early Defense vs Late Defense is a single technical trick.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: Treat it as a decision rule that appears across many positions.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Understanding the concept automatically makes it work live.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: The concept needs body signals, short cues, and positional rolling.

trainingCues: Name Early Defense vs Late Defense before adding force.
Find the body signal instead of guessing generally.
If structure is lost, reset one layer first.
Drill slowly, then test with progressive resistance.
